title: Book Club Reading Plan
aka: Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days
story: Your book club picked a novel and set a deadline: everyone finishes in days days. You know the page count of every chapter. You will read the chapters in order, never stop in the middle of one, and read at least one chapter on each reading day you use.
You want a daily page limit you can stick to every day. A low limit is easier on your evenings, but too low and you miss the deadline. What is the lowest limit that still works?
task: Write dailyPageLimit(chapters, days). Split chapters, in order, into at most days consecutive groups (each day reads one group). Return the smallest possible value of the largest group's page total.
Finishing early is fine, so using fewer than days days is allowed.

examples.explanation: Read 12 + 30 = 42, then 8 + 25 = 33, then 15 + 10 = 25. The busiest day is 42. With a limit of 41 you would need 4 days: 12 | 30 + 8 | 25 + 15 | 10. The average, 100 / 3 ≈ 34, is not achievable.
The 40-page chapter cannot be split, so the limit is at least 40. And 40 works: day 1 reads it, day 2 reads the other 30 pages.

hints: Forget finding the best split. If someone handed you a limit, say 41 for the first example, could you quickly tell whether 3 days are enough?

Yes: read greedily. Keep adding chapters to today until the next one would push you over the limit, then start a new day. Count the days. Reading as much as allowed each day can never make you need more days.
If a limit works, every larger limit works too. So the limits form a row of "too low" followed by "works". You want the first "works". What is the smallest limit worth trying, and the largest?

Binary search the limit between max(chapters) (you must fit the longest chapter) and sum(chapters) (everything in one day). For each middle limit, run the greedy day count. If it fits in days, keep it and search lower; otherwise search higher.
bruteForce: Try every limit from the longest chapter upward, running the greedy day count each time, and stop at the first one that fits. Or try every way to cut the chapters into groups.
Cutting is exponential. Counting up limits is O(n × S), where S can be up to 100,000,000 pages: far too many tries. Binary search on the limit needs about 27 tries, each a single O(n) pass.

js: * @param {number[]} chapters  page counts, read in this order
* @return {number} smallest daily page limit that finishes in time
py: def daily_page_limit(chapters: list[int], days: int) -> int:

tests.note: a long chapter at the end

js: // how many days does a given limit need, reading greedily?
if (today + pages > limit) { count++; today = 0; } // start a new day
let hi = chapters.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
if (daysNeeded(mid) <= days) hi = mid; // works: try lower

walkthrough: Finding the best split directly is hard. Checking a given limit is easy, and the answers are monotonic: once a limit works, every bigger one works. So binary search on the answer, using the easy check.
Trace [12, 30, 8, 25, 15, 10] with 3 days. The limit is somewhere between 30 (the longest chapter) and 100 (the total):

Start lo at the longest chapter, not at 1. Below that the greedy check is meaningless: a 30-page chapter can never fit under a 20-page limit, yet the loop above would happily put it on its own day and count it.
solution.timeWhy: About log₂ S binary search rounds, where S is the total page count, and each round is one O(n) greedy pass.
solution.takeaway: When the question is "the smallest X such that something is possible" and checking a given X is easy, binary search over X. The check is usually a simple greedy pass; the search range runs from the smallest value that could work to one that surely works.
